Because magnetic fields carry energy, doubling the field strength quadruples the stored energy density.

spatial-position-operator-component-e439.title: Spatial Position Operator Component
spatial-position-operator-component-e439.description: Represents the fundamental quantum observable corresponding to the $j$-th spatial coordinate of a particle, acting as a self-adjoint operator on the system Hilbert space.
spatial-position-operator-component-e439.conceptual_definition: The spatial position operator component $\hat{x}_j$ is defined by its spectral resolution $\hat{x}_j = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x_j |x_j\rangle \langle x_j| \, dx_j$. In the coordinate representation, its action on a state vector $\psi(\mathbf{r}) \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is given by pointwise multiplication: $(\hat{x}_j \psi)(\mathbf{r}) = x_j \psi(\mathbf{r})$.
spatial-position-operator-component-e439.interpretation: The operator $\hat{x}_j$ denotes the $j$-th Cartesian component ($j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$) of the vector position operator $\hat{\mathbf{r}}$. It is self-adjoint with a continuous spectrum spanning $\mathbb{R}$, satisfying the canonical commutation relations $[\hat{x}_j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\delta_{jk}\hat{I}$ with the conjugate momentum operator $\hat{p}_k$.
spatial-position-operator-component-e439.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit ($\hbar \to 0$), the commutator $[\hat{x}_j, \hat{p}_k] \to 0$, reducing quantum position operators to commuting canonical coordinates $x_j$ on classical phase space.
spatial-position-operator-component-e439.symmetry_origin: Under continuous spatial translations generated by the momentum operator $\hat{\mathbf{p}}$, the position operator transforms as $\hat{T}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{a}) \hat{\mathbf{x}} \hat{T}(\mathbf{a}) = \hat{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{a}$, reflecting the Euclidean translational symmetry of flat space.

position-from-variable-acceleration-80c9.title: Position from Variable Acceleration
position-from-variable-acceleration-80c9.description: This equation calculates the position vector of an object at time t by integrating its acceleration twice, and adding contributions from initial velocity and initial position. It is a fundamental kinematic equation for motion under variable acceleration.
position-from-variable-acceleration-80c9.conceptual_definition: The position vector of an object is determined by its initial position, the displacement from its initial velocity over time, and the cumulative displacement resulting from its time-varying acceleration. This is the general solution to the fundamental kinematic equation of motion $\mathbf{a}(t) = \mathrm{d}^2\mathbf{x}/\mathrm{d}t^2$.
position-from-variable-acceleration-80c9.interpretation: This equation provides the position vector $\mathbf{x}(t)$ at any time $t$, assuming the motion starts at $t=0$. The term $\mathbf{x}_0$ is the initial position vector, the starting point of the motion. The term $\mathbf{v}_0 t$ represents the displacement that would occur if the object moved at its constant initial velocity $\mathbf{v}_0$. The double integral term, $\int_{0}^{t} \int_{0}^{\tau} \mathbf{a}(\tau') \mathrm{d}\tau' \mathrm{d}\tau$, calculates the additional displacement due to the acceleration $\mathbf{a}(t)$. The inner integral, $\int_{0}^{\tau} \mathbf{a}(\tau') \mathrm{d}\tau'$, finds the change in velocity from time $0$ to an intermediate time $\tau$. The outer integral then sums up the displacement caused by this continuously changing velocity over the full duration from $0$ to $t$. The use of definite integrals and distinct integration variables ($\tau, \tau'$) ensures mathematical rigor.
position-from-variable-acceleration-80c9.limits_and_boundary:
1. Non-relativistic limit: The formula is valid only for speeds $v \ll c$, where $c$ is the speed of light, within the domain of classical mechanics.
2. Constant acceleration: If $\mathbf{a}(t)$ is a constant vector $\mathbf{a}$, the double integral evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$, recovering the standard kinematic equation $\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}_0 + \mathbf{v}_0 t + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$.
3. Zero acceleration: If $\mathbf{a}(t) = 0$, the equation simplifies to motion with constant velocity, $\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}_0 + \mathbf{v}_0 t$.
4. Initial conditions: The formula requires the initial position $\mathbf{x}_0$ and initial velocity $\mathbf{v}_0$ at a specified initial time (here, $t=0$) as boundary conditions.
position-from-variable-acceleration-80c9.symmetry_origin: The equation's structure is rooted in the fundamental symmetries of spacetime in classical mechanics. Time translation invariance (homogeneity of time), which implies the laws of physics are constant in time, leads to the conservation of energy and allows for a well-defined integration process. The existence of the integration constants $\mathbf{x}_0$ and $\mathbf{v}_0$ is a direct result of this time translation symmetry for the underlying second-order differential equation. Similarly, the vector nature of the equation respects the homogeneity and isotropy of space.

information-per-subsystem-dimension-873c.title: Quantum Information Density per Subsystem Dimension
information-per-subsystem-dimension-873c.description: Measures the average quantum or mutual information localized within a subsystem normalized by the dimension of its underlying Hilbert space.
information-per-subsystem-dimension-873c.conceptual_definition: The information per subsystem dimension $\mathcal{I}_{d} = \frac{I}{d_S}$ normalizes a designated information metric $I$ (such as quantum mutual information, von Neumann entropy, or accessible information) by the finite dimension $d_S = \dim(\mathcal{H}_S)$ of the subsystem's state space. This characterizes the density of quantum correlations or encoded information per orthogonal basis state of the subsystem.
information-per-subsystem-dimension-873c.interpretation: In composite quantum architectures, the total information $I$ shared by a subsystem $S$ scales with its size, but Hilbert space dimension $d_S$ grows exponentially with particle number $N$ ($d_S = 2^N$ for qubits). The quantity $I/d_S$ indicates whether quantum correlations are concentrated into a few key degrees of freedom or diluted across the exponentially large state space.
information-per-subsystem-dimension-873c.limits_and_boundary: For a maximally entangled subsystem of dimension $d_S$, the maximum entropy is $I_{\max} = \ln d_S$, yielding $\lim_{d_S \to \infty} \frac{\ln d_S}{d_S} = 0$. For a trivial 1-dimensional subspace ($d_S = 1$), the quantity reduces identically to zero as no quantum information can be stored.
information-per-subsystem-dimension-873c.symmetry_origin: Invariance under local unitary transformations $U_S \in \mathrm{U}(d_S)$ acting on the subsystem Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_S$, preserving both the subsystem dimension $d_S$ and spectral information invariants.

right-handed-up-quark-adjoint-spinor-2ff.title: Right-Handed Up Quark Adjoint Spinor
right-handed-up-quark-adjoint-spinor-2ff.description: Represents the Dirac adjoint (conjugate) of the right-handed up quark field, defined as $\b\bar{u}}_R = u_R^\dagger \gamma^0 = \b\bar{u}} P_L$, which serves as a fundamental building block for Lorentz-invariant Yukawa couplings and gauge currents in the Standard Model.
right-handed-up-quark-adjoint-spinor-2ff.conceptual_definition: The right-handed up quark adjoint spinor $\b\bar{u}}_R$ is constructed by taking the Hermitian conjugate of the right-chiral up quark field $u_R = P_R u$ and contracting it with the zeroth Dirac gamma matrix $\gamma^0$. Because $\gamma^0 P_R = P_L \gamma^0$, the adjoint of a right-handed chiral field transforms under Lorentz boosts and rotations with left-handed projector properties, $\b\bar{u}}_R = \b\bar{u}} P_L$. It transforms as a singlet under the electroweak gauge group $SU(2)_L$ with weak hypercharge $Y = +4/3$ (or $+2/3$ depending on normalization) and in the anti-fundamental $\mathbf{\bar{3}}$ representation of color $SU(3)_C$.
right-handed-up-quark-adjoint-spinor-2ff.interpretation: In quantum field theory, the operator $\b\bar{u}}_R$ acts on Fock space states: it destroys a right-handed up quark $u_R$ with helicity $+1/2$ (in the massless limit) or creates an anti-up quark $\b\bar{u}}$ with left-handed helicity $-1/2$. In the Standard Model Lagrangian, $\b\bar{u}}_R$ couples to the left-handed quark doublet $Q_L = (u_L, d_L)^T$ via the Higgs doublet conjugate $\tilde{\Phi}$ through the up-type Yukawa interaction $-y_u \bar{Q}_L \tilde{\Phi} u_R + \text{h.c.}$, which generates the Dirac mass of the up quark upon electroweak symmetry breaking.
right-handed-up-quark-adjoint-spinor-2ff.limits_and_boundary: In the ultra-relativistic limit $E \gg m_u$ (or massless limit $m_u \to 0$), chirality corresponds exactly to helicity; $\b\bar{u}}_R$ strictly projects onto positive helicity quark annihilation and negative helicity antiquark creation operators. In the non-relativistic limit $p/m_u \to 0$, chirality and helicity decouple, and the spinor representation reduces to standard Pauli 2-spinor components.
right-handed-up-quark-adjoint-spinor-2ff.symmetry_origin: Under the Standard Model gauge group $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$, the conjugate field $\b\bar{u}}_R$ transforms in the $(\mathbf{\bar{3}}, \mathbf{1}, -2/3)$ representation under electric charge conventions, ensuring gauge invariance when contracted with left-handed doublets and the Higgs scalar field.

cosmological-jerk-parameter-definition-b.title: Cosmological Jerk Parameter Definition
cosmological-jerk-parameter-definition-b.description: This equation defines the dimensionless cosmological jerk parameter 'j' in terms of the scale factor 'a' and its first and third derivatives with respect to cosmic time.
cosmological-jerk-parameter-definition-b.conceptual_definition: The jerk parameter, denoted $j$, is a dimensionless cosmological quantity that characterizes the third derivative of the cosmic scale factor $a$ with respect to cosmic time $t$. It quantifies the rate of change of the cosmic acceleration, providing a higher-order description of the universe's expansion dynamics. In the context of the Friedmann equations, it offers insight into how the acceleration itself evolves over cosmic history.
cosmological-jerk-parameter-definition-b.interpretation: The jerk parameter $j$ is a crucial diagnostic in physical cosmology, particularly for distinguishing between various dark energy models and modified gravity theories. While the Hubble parameter describes the expansion rate and the deceleration parameter describes the acceleration, $j$ describes the rate at which this acceleration changes. For the standard Lambda-CDM model, the jerk parameter is constant and equal to 1. Deviations from j=1 can indicate alternative cosmological models, providing a way to test the standard model against observations. It helps to characterize the 'smoothness' and complexity of the universe's expansion history.
cosmological-jerk-parameter-definition-b.limits_and_boundary: This equation is applicable within the framework of homogeneous and isotropic cosmological models (Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric).
